Alloying Error Prompts 2022 to 2026 Toyota Tundra Exhaust Camshaft Recall
32 photos
Photo: Toyota / edited
Toyota's half-ton pickup faces a new recall, and the problem with the subject population boils down to a manufacturing mistake that should have never made it past quality control. Toyota claims the camshaft supplier added alloy additives twice during the production of a 400-piece batch, pushing magnesium content way beyond Toyota's specifications.
Magnesium is a strong carbide stabilizer, forcing the formation of brittle intercellular iron carbides. Subsequent machining created small cracks in those 400 exhaust-side cams, and those cracks are certain to grow in time until they break. Such a failure would automatically result in a loss of motive power, increasing the risk of a crash.
Toyota initially estimated approximately 300 potentially affected cams. The media release published by the world's largest automaker is pretty lacking in terms of details, but on the other hand, the Part 573 safety recall report published by the NHTSA answers most curiosities. For example, 13502-F4010 is the part number of the subject bank one exhaust camshaft.
CWC Textron is listed as the supplier, and the recall population is split between 2022 - 2023 and 2025 - 2026 models. Unfortunately, the Part 573 report fails to explain why 2024 models are not included. In the United States market, no fewer than 62,490 Tundras are being recalled. Hybrids need not apply.
Given that only 400 cams have been produced incorrectly, it goes without saying that fewer than 1 percent of the vehicle population features iffy exhaust cams. The 2025 - 2026 trucks could have received suspect components during production, while older Tundras could have received them as part of a service replacement.
Photo: Toyota The population splits between 17,762 older trucks and 44,728 newer vehicles. In principle, an exhaust cam isn't a terribly complicated piece of kit. Cams rotate in sync with the crankshaft of the twin-turbo V6 engine, and exhaust cams are designed to operate the exhaust valves. Basically, these parts control when spent gases leave the combustion chambers.
Thousands of revolutions per minute is tough on those cams, and that's why the alloy has to be perfectly so for each application. Cracking under repeated mechanical loads is a big no-no. When that happens, a bunch of warning lights may illuminate. Under the hood, the engine may run rougher than normal, misfire, or stall without warning.
The first warning came in October 2025, when Toyota Motor North America received a report alleging a no-start condition and an illuminated warning light. Technicians recovered the engine, tore it apart, and found that its right-hand exhaust cam had snapped. A second report arrived in December of last year, with TMNA finding surface cracks and another broken cam.
Material analysis provided the first useful clue, prompting Toyota Motor North America to contact the supplier. CWC Textron determined that an operator manually added the alloy additives a second time, apparently unaware that the automated system had already accounted for them. The mistake occurred during a shutdown of a casting line due to equipment issues.
All tested components exceeded the internal magnesium limits. By October 30, 2026, Toyota Motor North America had counted 60 warranty claims and 31 field technical reports in the United States of America. Affected owners will be notified by the Japanese automaker between December 28, 2026, and January 11, 2027.
